problem.text: For certain real numbers $a$, $b$, and $c$, the polynomial $$g(x) = x^3 + ax^2 + x + 10$$ has three distinct roots, and each root of $g(x)$ is also a root of the polynomial $$f(x) = x^4 + x^3 + bx^2 + 100x + c.$$ What is $f(1)$?

steps.title: Where to start: $g(x)$ divides $f(x)$
steps.body: Each of the three distinct roots of $g$ is a root of $f$, so $f$ has a factor $(x - \text{root})$ for each of them, and their product is exactly $g(x)$. Since $f$ has degree $4$ and $g$ has degree $3$, one more linear factor is left. Call the fourth root of $f$ by the letter $r$, so $f(x) = g(x)\,(x - r)$.

your_turn.prompt: Why is the extra factor $(x - r)$ and not, say, $2(x - r)$?
your_turn.answer: Both $f$ and $g$ have leading coefficient $1$, so the leftover factor must also have leading coefficient $1$.

steps.title: Expand the product
steps.body:
Multiply out $(x^3 + ax^2 + x + 10)(x - r)$ and collect powers of $x$:
$$x^4 + (a - r)x^3 + (1 - ar)x^2 + (10 - r)x - 10r$$
This must equal $x^4 + x^3 + bx^2 + 100x + c$ term by term.

your_turn.prompt: Match the $x$ terms. Which equation do you get, and what is $r$?

steps.title: Find the other letters
steps.body: Now match the rest: the $x^3$ terms give $a - r = 1$, the constants give $c = -10r$, and the $x^2$ terms give $b = 1 - ar$.
